| Regulatory basis | • Park managers or subdistrict offices are responsible for public-space waste management, appropriate container provision, timely collection and cleanliness to prevent overflow and accumulation. Regulations on Urban Appearance and Environmental Sanitation Management, Article 12.<br>• Littering and dumping or stockpiling outside designated areas, including water, planting and paths, are prohibited. Regulations on Urban Appearance and Environmental Sanitation Management, Article 16.<br>• Classification containers should be clearly labelled, intact and free of damage or spills; collection should adjust to generation to prevent overflow. Signs for classification of municipal solid wasteGB/T 19095-2019 Section 5.2.<br>• Public areas such as parks should establish daily checks and cleaning and address accumulation or overflow within 24 hours of discovery. Quality Standard for Urban Environmental Sanitation Operations (CJJ/T 275-2018), Section 6.3.2.<br>• Delayed collection causing overflow, accumulation, pollution or visual impacts may attract warnings, fines or suspension for rectification in serious cases, where collection duties are unfulfilled or management inadequate. Regulations on Urban Appearance and Environmental Sanitation Management, Article 36. |
| Severity | **Moderate.** One overflowing bin and five accumulations, including floating objects and misidentified animals, impair park cleanliness across paths and water with potential spread, without severe pollution or sanitation hazards. |
| Impact assessment | Visible effects: overflow scatters waste and impairs path appearance; floating objects may pollute water and affect the landscape. Pigeons misidentified as ground accumulation reveal system errors that may mislead management. Near-term risks include insects and odours from overflow, blocked drains or ecological effects from floating objects, and safety or sanitation concerns near children’s play facilities. |
| Potential causes | • Overflow may reflect delayed collection or a surge after holidays or events: S15-A-01 is beside a busy children’s ride. Verify collection frequency and recent events.<br>• Floating objects in S15-A-02 may be discarded or detached decorations, indicating management gaps or ageing facilities. Review monitoring or cleaning records.<br>• Pigeons in S15-A-03 may be misidentified because the model poorly distinguishes animals and waste. Review annotation rules and animal examples in training data.<br>• Dispersed problems may reflect inadequate dynamic checks or collection scheduling. Verify park cleaning and collection registers. |
| Long-term effects | Persistent or recurrent problems could reduce park quality and visitor experience, encourage insects and pathogens, increase health risks, damage aquatic ecology and landscape functions, and cause complaints or adverse environmental assessments if responsibilities remain unfulfilled. |
| Recommendations | • Immediate action: empty S15-A-01 and clear scattered waste; retrieve S15-A-02 floating objects and determine whether they are damaged decorations or litter; sweep S15-A-03 and verify animal misidentification; and check S15-A-04 collection records.<br>• Longer-term action: adjust collection to visitor peaks, strengthen pond and planted-area checks, calibrate the AI system using non-waste examples such as animals and decorations, and link problem locations, response and feedback within park-management assessment. |
| Priority | **Medium.** Overflow and accumulation affect cleanliness in sensitive play and water areas without major pollution or safety risks. Complete action within 24–48 hours to avoid escalation or complaints. |
